paras: The threatened lynching of Perry Griffin took place on 13 July 1903 in Mount Vernon, New York, when a crowd surrounded Griffin, a 23-year-old Black coachman, crying "Lynch him" after he shot and killed another Black coachman, Eli Brown, in front of the City Hall. Six policemen escorted Griffin through the crowd to the station house, and he was later held in the White Plains jail to await trial for murder. The story ran in New York dailies and, through a short wire report, in papers in other states, with headlines that credited the police with keeping the crowd from the prisoner.

Griffin worked as coachman for a Dr. Ronaldson, and Brown, 25, drove for Minot C. Kellogg, described as a bank president. The New York papers called the shooting the end of "an old feud" that Griffin attributed to Brown's attentions to his wife. According to the Evening World, Griffin told police he had repeatedly warned Brown to stay away.

Shortly before or after 3 o'clock that afternoon, as people moved in and out of the City Hall, Griffin met Brown in the street and fired at him with a revolver. The shooting took place in sight of about 500 excursionists on trolley cars bound for Glen Island. Brown, hit in the head, cried "Now, you have killed me!" and fell dead.

Griffin ran and was overtaken by Eugene Fisher, whom the Evening World called a detective and the Tribune a former detective. The Evening World reported that Griffin fired at Fisher and missed, while the Tribune gave this as Fisher's own account. With help from people in the crowd, Fisher subdued Griffin and dragged him into the City Hall, where he was turned over to Patrolman Marz.

As Griffin was led to the station house, a crowd surrounded him crying "Lynch him" and pressed in so closely that the police on several occasions "had to make a show of force." The Tribune wrote that "at one time it was feared that the murderer would be lynched," and that it took six policemen to guard him from the "furious" crowd. No report describes an attempt to seize the prisoner, and the crowd's makeup and race are not given.

Griffin was locked up at police headquarters charged with murder. Coroner Weisendanger opened an inquest the same night and heard a dozen witnesses, who said Brown "made no motion" and did no overt act, and that Griffin had bought the revolver about half an hour before the shooting. In September the Tribune listed "Perry Griffen, a colored man," among six accused killers awaiting trial in the White Plains jail, where District Attorney Young was preparing the cases. No report of a trial or verdict was found.

The Evening World, publishing the same afternoon, built its headlines around the crowd: "Police Keep Angry Crowd from Slayer" and "'Lynch Him!' Cried Crowd Surrounding Prisoner." The next morning the Tribune and the Sun ran nearly identical stories headlined as a murder before 500 excursionists, mentioning the lynching fear in a single clause. Both papers printed Griffin's claim that Brown had pulled a stone, though only the Tribune added the inquest testimony that contradicted it.

A short wire version, which garbled Griffin's name as "Terry Griffin" or "Terry Griggin," ran on 14 July in Perth Amboy, New Haven, Portland and Worcester. Its headlines ranged from "Negro Kills Negro at Mount Vernon" and "Cold Blooded Murder" to the Worcester Spy's "Policeman Prevented Negro Being Lynched." All of the known reports appeared in white dailies, and no Black-press account appears in the coverage.

Accounts of the shooting differ on the number of shots: the Evening World and the Sun say three bullets struck Brown's head, while the Tribune's headline and Griffin's own words give four. Griffin's claim that Brown threatened him with a stone rests on his own statement, against the inquest witnesses' testimony that Brown made no move.

A crowd threatened to lynch Griffin over the killing of Eli Brown, but police kept him in custody and no one was killed by the crowd (A1, A2, A4); the only death was Brown's, shot by Griffin, not a lynching.
The Evening World, the Tribune, the Sun and a separate wire report all describe the shooting and the crowd's lynching threat, with six policemen guarding the prisoner (A1, A2, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Evening World local report
accounts.gist: Griffin shot Brown without a word, fired at the pursuing detective, and was led through a 'clamoring throng' crying 'Lynch him' by six policemen who had to make a show of force.

accounts.label: Griffin's statement
accounts.gist: Griffin said Brown had been too attentive to his wife and that Brown pulled a stone from his pocket, so he fired in fear.

accounts.label: Coroner's inquest witnesses
accounts.gist: A dozen witnesses said Brown made no motion and did no overt act; Griffin had bought the revolver half an hour earlier and was calling Brown names before firing.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A large crowd gathered, Griffin was captured at once and taken to headquarters under a guard of six policemen because it was feared the excited crowd might attempt lynching.

framing.detail: The Evening World led with the police protection, 'Police Keep Angry Crowd from Slayer' and '"Lynch Him!" Cried Crowd Surrounding Prisoner', while calling Griffin 'the slayer' and 'the murderer'.
The Tribune and the Sun framed it as a murder before 500 excursionists, mentioning the lynching fear in a single clause.
The wire story ran under headlines from 'Negro Kills Negro at Mount Vernon' to 'Policeman Prevented Negro Being Lynched'.
